# Pranjul Rathour

> GenAI engineering, hackathons and campus talks, answered from experience. Written by Pranjul Rathour, GenAI engineer in Kanpur, India (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com). Each page answers real search questions about one topic, cites primary sources, and draws on production systems he shipped (RAG.NextUpgrad, FineTune Studio, DocuLens AI, FaceVision, OCR & Speech Workspace) and three hackathon first prizes.

- [About Pranjul Rathour](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/about/): bio, experience, awards, sessions delivered
- [Contact](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/contact/): email and every profile
- [Invite Pranjul to your campus](https://pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite): talks, workshops, hackathon judging and mentoring; book at https://pranjulrathour.scult.in/book
- [FAQ](https://pranjulrathour.scult.in/faq): inviting, hiring, booking and about, answered; full text at https://pranjulrathour.scult.in/llms-full.txt

## Travel, stay and fees for campus sessions

For campus sessions the inviting institution covers the visit end to end: travel (a First AC train ticket for journeys up to five hours, a flight for anything longer), accommodation, meals, and pickup and drop. The honorarium and workshop fees are negotiable on WhatsApp or on the call; requests are welcome from institutions that can cover the visit this way. Details: https://pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite#travel

## RAG & retrieval

Retrieval-augmented generation, vector search and grounded answers, from a production platform.

- [What is machine learning, and what is it actually used for? The three types, how it differs from AI and deep learning, and real applications](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-machine-learning/): Machine learning is software that improves at a task from data instead of following rules a programmer wrote by hand. Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning explained plainly, how ML relates to AI and deep learning, and where it is genuinely used today, from spam filters to the models behind modern generative AI.
- [What is a vector database? How vector search works, when you need one, and FAISS vs pgvector vs Qdrant vs Pinecone](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-vector-database/): A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones fast. How vector search and ANN indexes work, when a library or Postgres is enough, and how to choose between FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Chroma, Weaviate, Pinecone and Milvus.
- [What is an LLM? Large language models explained: tokens, context windows, parameters, open vs closed models, and what they cost to run](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-llm/): A large language model predicts the next token, and everything else follows from that. How LLMs are trained, what parameters, tokens and context windows mean, how GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama and Mistral differ, what hallucination is, how to run one locally, and how to reason about cost. Written from shipping LLM products.
- [How to evaluate a RAG system: recall, faithfulness, RAGAS, building a test set and the metrics that actually predict user complaints](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-evaluate-a-rag-system/): Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. How to build a labelled question set from real usage, measure recall at k and MRR for retrieval, faithfulness and answer relevance for generation, use RAGAS and LLM judges without fooling yourself, run evaluation in CI, and read the numbers that predict whether users will trust the system. From a production RAG platform with 196 tests.
- [Hybrid search and reranking in RAG: BM25 plus embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoders, and why this pair fixes most bad answers](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-and-reranking-in-rag/): Why vector search alone misses exact terms and keyword search alone misses meaning, how to fuse them with reciprocal rank fusion in a dozen lines, what a cross-encoder reranker does and why it beats retrieving more, how to tune k at each stage, how to measure the gain with recall, and how the hybrid path works in a production RAG platform.
- [RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering: which one your problem actually needs, with a decision tree and real costs](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning/): RAG supplies knowledge at answer time; fine-tuning changes behaviour; prompting steers both. When each wins, when to combine them, what each costs to build and maintain, the failure modes, and the decision tree I use with clients after building both a RAG platform and a fine-tuning platform in the same year.
- [What are embeddings in AI? Text embeddings, vector similarity, choosing a model, and how embeddings power RAG and semantic search](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-embeddings-in-ai/): An embedding turns text, an image or audio into a vector so that similar things are close together. How embedding models are trained, what dimensions and similarity mean, how embeddings differ from tokens, how to choose and evaluate a model with MTEB, and how they are used in RAG, search, clustering and recommendation.
- [What is agentic RAG and Graph RAG? Query rewriting, multi-step retrieval, knowledge graphs, and when a plain RAG pipeline is not enough](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-agentic-rag-and-graph-rag/): Agentic RAG puts a planning loop around retrieval: rewrite the query, choose among retrievers, check results, retrieve again. Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph over documents and retrieves through entities and communities. What each adds, what each costs, HyDE, Self-RAG, RAPTOR and corrective patterns, and how to decide whether your system needs any of it. From a production RAG platform that mostly does not.
- [What is chunking in RAG? Chunk size, overlap, structure-aware splitting and the experiments that actually decide retrieval quality](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chunking-in-rag/): Chunking splits documents into retrievable passages, and it decides RAG quality more than the model does. Fixed, recursive, semantic, structure-aware and parent-child chunking compared, how to choose chunk size and overlap from your own questions, how to chunk PDFs, tables and code, and the mistakes that make retrieval fail.
- [What is a context window, and what is context engineering? Token limits, why bigger isn't always better, and deciding what a model actually sees](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-context-window-and-context-engineering/): A context window is the maximum amount of text, in tokens, a model can hold in one call: the prompt, retrieved documents, conversation history and the answer all share this one budget. What happens when you exceed it, why a huge context window doesn't remove the need for retrieval, the lost-in-the-middle effect, and context engineering, the discipline of deciding exactly what enters that budget and in what order.
- [What is RAG in AI? Retrieval-augmented generation, explained from a production system](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-ai/): RAG gives a language model documents to read before it answers. What it is, how the pipeline works, when to use it instead of fine-tuning, and how I built one that refuses to guess.

## Fine-tuning LLMs

LoRA, QLoRA, datasets, loss curves and evaluation, from building a fine-tuning platform.

- [Data analyst vs machine learning engineer vs AI engineer: what each job actually does, the skill overlap, and which path fits you](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/data-analyst-vs-ai-ml-engineer-career-path/): Three career paths students often confuse because they share tools: data analyst, machine learning engineer, and AI or GenAI engineer. What each role does day to day, the real skill overlap and where it ends, typical entry points from a BCA, B.Tech or MCA background, and how to decide between them without guessing from job titles alone.
- [How to fine-tune an LLM: LoRA, QLoRA, datasets and evaluation, from building a fine-tuning platform](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-fine-tune-an-llm/): What fine-tuning an LLM means, when it beats RAG or prompting, how LoRA and QLoRA make it fit on a free GPU, how to prepare a dataset, read the loss curve and evaluate honestly.
- [How to prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM: formats, chat templates, how much data, synthetic data, validation and the checklist before you train](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prepare-a-dataset-for-fine-tuning/): The dataset is the fine-tune. How to write a spec, choose between Alpaca, ShareGPT and chat formats, apply the model's chat template correctly, decide how many examples you need, generate and filter synthetic data, deduplicate, split, and validate every row before spending a GPU hour. From building a fine-tuning platform.
- [LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning: memory, speed, quality and cost compared, with the settings that matter and how to fine-tune on a free Colab GPU](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/lora-vs-qlora/): The practical differences between LoRA, QLoRA and full fine-tuning: how much VRAM each needs for 1B to 70B models, how fast they train, how quality compares, which to choose for your task and hardware, the rank, alpha and target-module settings that matter, and a free-GPU recipe. From building a fine-tuning platform that runs QLoRA from the browser.
- [What is overfitting in machine learning, and how do you actually prevent it? Train/validation/test splits, regularization, and catching it early](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-overfitting-and-how-to-prevent-it/): Overfitting is when a model learns the training data instead of the pattern behind it: great training accuracy, poor performance on anything new. What causes it, how a proper train/validation/test split catches it, the standard prevention techniques, regularization, dropout, early stopping, more data, and how the same failure shows up, and is fixed differently, when fine-tuning an LLM specifically.
- [What is quantization in LLMs? 4-bit and 8-bit models, GGUF vs AWQ vs GPTQ, quality loss, and running big models on small hardware](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-quantization-in-llms/): Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits so LLMs fit in less memory and run faster. How it works, what INT8, INT4, NF4 and GGUF mean, how GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ differ and when to use each, how much quality you lose, how it relates to QLoRA, and how to quantize your own fine-tuned model for a laptop or a server.
- [What is RLHF, instruction tuning and DPO? How base models become assistants, what alignment training actually does, and when a small team should use it](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rlhf-instruction-tuning-and-dpo/): How a raw language model that only predicts the next token becomes a helpful assistant: supervised instruction tuning on demonstrations, reinforcement learning from human feedback with a reward model, and the direct preference methods (DPO, ORPO, KTO, GRPO) that replaced most of the RL machinery. What each stage changes, what the data looks like, the costs, the failure modes such as reward hacking and sycophancy, and the honest answer to whether a student or small team should do preference tuning at all.

## Vision, speech & OCR

Face recognition, liveness, document AI, speech-to-text and on-device inference.

- [What is computer vision? How machines see images, the classic pipeline versus deep learning, and where it's used, from cameras to medical scans](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-computer-vision/): Computer vision is the field of getting machines to extract meaning from images and video: what is in the picture, where it is, and what is happening. How it evolved from hand-engineered features to convolutional networks to vision transformers, the core tasks (classification, detection, segmentation, tracking), where it is genuinely used today, and how it relates to the vision-language models that now sit alongside it.
- [How does face recognition work? Detection, embeddings, thresholds and liveness, from building FaceVision](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-face-recognition-work/): Face detection finds faces; face recognition turns each face into an embedding and compares distances against a threshold; liveness detection stops a photo from passing. How each step works, why systems fail on twins and low light, how accurate they are, the privacy rules, and how I built a browser-only version that never uploads a face.
- [How does OCR work? From Tesseract to document AI: turning scanned PDFs and invoices into searchable, structured text](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-ocr-work/): OCR turns images of text into text. How the pipeline works, where Tesseract still fits, how vision-language models changed document AI, how to OCR a PDF for free, how to extract invoice fields you can trust, and how I built a page-batched OCR and speech workspace on Mistral.
- [How does speech to text work? Whisper, real-time transcription architecture, Indian languages, and building a live transcription feature](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-speech-to-text-work/): How automatic speech recognition turns audio into text, what changed with Whisper, how to build real-time transcription with streaming and voice activity detection, how to handle Hindi and mixed-language speech, the accuracy metric that matters, and how I built a live speech-to-text feature into a document workspace.
- [What are vision-language models and multimodal AI? How VLMs see images, what they can and cannot do, and building student projects with them](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-vision-language-models/): Vision-language models take images and text together and answer in text: describe a photo, read a chart, extract fields from a form, answer questions about a diagram. How they work, from CLIP to today's multimodal LLMs, what they are good and bad at, how they compare with classic vision models, what they cost, and five student projects that go beyond chat with a PDF.
- [What is edge AI and on-device AI? Running models in the browser and on phones with ONNX Runtime, WebGPU and quantization, from building a browser-only face recognition system](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-edge-ai-and-on-device-ai/): Edge AI runs models where the data is, on phones, laptops, browsers and small devices, instead of in the cloud. Why it matters for privacy, latency and cost, how ONNX Runtime Web and WebGPU make browser inference practical, what fits on a device, how to export and quantize a model, and how FaceVision keeps every camera frame on the user's machine.
- [What is object detection? YOLO explained, detection vs classification vs segmentation, training on your own data, and running it in real time on a budget GPU](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-object-detection-yolo/): Object detection finds and labels every object in an image with a box. How YOLO-style detectors work in one pass, how detection differs from classification and segmentation, how mAP and IoU are measured, how to train a detector on your own images, how to run it in real time on cheap hardware or in the browser, and the mistakes that produce a demo that fails on real cameras.

## Shipping AI apps

Agents, prompts, costs, security and deployment for AI products that survive real users.

- [What is prompt engineering? Techniques that work, system prompts, prompt injection, and whether it is still a job](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-prompt-engineering/): Prompt engineering is writing and testing the instructions a language model runs on. The techniques that hold up, how system prompts differ from user prompts, what prompt injection is and how to defend against it, how to learn it, and where it sits next to RAG, agents and fine-tuning.
- [What is vibe coding? AI coding assistants explained, Cursor vs Copilot vs Claude Code, when it works, when it fails, and how to use it without losing your skills](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vibe-coding/): Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI assistant and accepting what it produces. What the term means, how coding agents differ from autocomplete, which tools students should learn, the projects it suits and the ones it wrecks, the review habits that keep it safe, and whether it makes learning to code pointless. From shipping production systems with and without assistants.
- [Do you actually need a GPU for AI? A plain VRAM and hardware guide for students: what runs on a laptop, what needs to be rented, and what needs neither](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/do-you-need-a-gpu-for-ai-vram-and-hardware-guide/): Most AI work a student does does not need a personal GPU at all. What actually needs local GPU memory versus what an API or a free cloud notebook already covers, how much VRAM common tasks need, quantization's effect on fitting a model into less memory, and a plain decision guide before spending money on hardware or a cloud GPU rental.
- [FastAPI for AI applications: async endpoints for LLM calls, dependency injection, streaming responses, and the patterns that hold up in production](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-for-ai-applications/): Why FastAPI is the default choice for serving LLM and RAG applications in Python: async request handling that does not block on slow model calls, dependency injection for clean provider and database wiring, background tasks for long-running jobs, streaming responses for token-by-token output, and the request lifecycle mistakes that quietly break concurrency. From the FastAPI layer behind a production RAG platform and a document extraction service.
- [How much does an LLM API cost? Token pricing explained, a cost model you can run, and 12 ways to cut the bill without cutting quality](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-much-does-an-llm-api-cost/): LLM APIs charge per million tokens, input and output priced separately. How to estimate the monthly cost of a feature before you build it, why RAG prompts are expensive, what prompt caching, batching, routing and smaller models save, when self-hosting an open model is cheaper, and the caps and alerts that stop a viral day from becoming a bill. From running five production AI apps on tight budgets.
- [How to build an AI app and deploy it for free: architecture, stack, hosting, costs and the checklist that survives real users](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-an-ai-app/): The architecture of an LLM app, a Python and FastAPI stack that ships in a weekend, free hosting options that still work in 2026, how to keep API costs predictable, the security and logging every AI app needs, and the mistakes that kill student projects after demo day. From shipping five production AI apps in six months.
- [How to structure an LLM project in Python: folder layout, config, prompts as files, evals, and the patterns that survive past the notebook](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-structure-an-llm-project-in-python/): The project structure for a Python LLM application that stays maintainable after the first demo: a src layout with clear modules for providers, prompts, retrieval and evaluation, typed settings from environment variables, prompts stored as versioned files, structured outputs with Pydantic, a golden test set and an eval command, logging that makes failures debuggable, and packaging for deployment. From the layouts used in a production RAG platform and a document extraction system.
- [Redis and caching strategies for LLM apps: exact-match caching, semantic caching, and what to cache when every model call costs money and time](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/redis-and-caching-strategies-for-llm-apps/): A cache hit on an LLM call is nearly free; a miss costs real money and real seconds. Exact-match caching with Redis, semantic caching for near-duplicate questions, what to cache safely and what never to cache, cache invalidation for RAG when source documents change, and the latency and cost numbers that make caching worth building before you need it.
- [System design for AI applications: how to answer 'design a RAG system' or 'design an AI agent' in an interview, and how to actually build one](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/system-design-for-ai-applications/): AI system design interviews ask you to design a RAG chatbot, a document-processing pipeline, or an agentic system under real constraints: latency, cost, scale, failure modes. The framework: clarify requirements, sketch the pipeline, name the hard trade-offs, then go deep on the two or three components that actually matter. Worked through a RAG system and an agent example, with the failure modes interviewers are listening for.
- [ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot: what each one actually is, who makes it, what it's for, and how to tell them apart](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-chatgpt-claude-gemini-copilot/): A plain-language guide to the AI assistants everyone mentions: what ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and GitHub/Microsoft Copilot actually are, who builds each one, what each is best at, why ChatGPT or Copilot sometimes goes down, what Claude Code and Codex are, and how to pick the right one for a task instead of defaulting to whichever is loudest.
- [What is an AI agent? Agentic AI explained: tools, function calling, MCP, frameworks, and why most agents fail](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent/): An AI agent is a language model in a loop with tools: it plans, acts, observes and repeats until a goal is met. What agentic AI means versus generative AI, how tool calling and the Model Context Protocol work, which frameworks to use, how to build one, and the guardrails that keep it from doing damage.
- [What is function calling (tool use) in LLMs? How models call your code, structured outputs, and building a reliable tool-using agent](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-function-calling-and-tool-use-in-llms/): Function calling, also called tool use, lets a language model request that your code run a specific function with specific arguments, rather than only returning text. How the model decides to call a tool, how the JSON schema contract works, why the same mechanism produces structured outputs and agents, and the reliability patterns, validation, retries, timeouts, that keep a tool-using system from silently breaking in production.
- [What is generative AI, and where can you actually learn it for free? A clear definition and a vetted list of free courses and certificates](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-generative-ai-and-where-to-learn-it-free/): Generative AI creates new content, text, images, audio, code, video, rather than only classifying or predicting from existing data. What separates it from classic machine learning and from a single LLM, where it is used, and a filtered list of genuinely free courses and certificates from Google, Microsoft, DeepLearning.AI, Hugging Face and Anthropic, with what each actually covers and how long each takes.
- [What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol? How MCP servers work, MCP vs function calling vs APIs, and how to build one, from running a public server](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol/): The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets any AI application use tools, data and prompts from any compliant server. How the client, server and host fit together, what tools, resources and prompts are, how MCP differs from function calling and plain APIs, the security model, how to build and test a server, and lessons from running a public MCP server at tools.scult.in.
- [What is vLLM? vLLM vs Ollama vs llama.cpp vs SGLang, and how to actually serve an LLM in production](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vllm-ollama-and-llm-inference-serving/): Running a model in a notebook and serving it to real traffic are different problems. vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp all serve LLMs but solve different problems: throughput at scale, ease of local use, or portability. What continuous batching and PagedAttention actually do, when each tool is the right choice, how much throughput difference it makes, and how to size a serving setup for real requests per second.

## Hackathons

Ideas, pitches, demos and judging, from three first prizes and the judge's table.

- [Hackathon judging criteria and a rubric organisers can copy: how judges score, how to brief a panel, how to break ties, and how to judge fairly in 15 minutes per team](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-judging-criteria-and-rubric/): The four criteria most hackathon rubrics reduce to, with weights, score anchors and the questions that reveal each; a 15-minute judging protocol; how to brief judges and handle conflicts of interest; tie-breaking; feedback that helps teams; and how to become a judge. From judging and briefing panels at college hackathons and winning three.
- [Hackathon pitch deck template: the seven slides, the three-minute script, demo rules and what judges score, from three first prizes and the judging table](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-pitch-deck-template/): A hackathon presentation that fits in three minutes: seven slides in the order judges want, what goes on each, a word-for-word script skeleton, how to demo without a crash, how to answer Q&A, and the mistakes that lose otherwise strong teams. Includes the Smart India Hackathon adaptation. From a builder with three first prizes who also judges.
- [Hackathon project ideas that win: 40 AI and software ideas for students, with the hard part of each, from three first prizes](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-project-ideas/): Forty hackathon project ideas across AI, agriculture, education, health, campus life and fintech, each with the user, the demo and the hard technical part named, plus how to pick one, how to adapt it to a problem statement, and what judges reward. From a builder with three first prizes and time on the judging panel.
- [How to participate in your first hackathon: where to find hackathons in India, how to form a team, what to prepare, and what to expect in 24 to 48 hours](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-participate-in-your-first-hackathon/): A beginner's guide to hackathons for students: where hackathons are listed (Devfolio, Unstop, MLH, Devpost, Hack2skill, Smart India Hackathon), how to register and get shortlisted, how to find teammates when you know nobody, what to install and prepare the week before, what the 24 to 48 hours actually feel like, what beginners should build, and how to make the first one count even if you do not win. From a first hackathon that went badly and three that were won later.
- [How to win a hackathon: what judges score, how to pick an idea, and the demo that works live, from three first prizes](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-a-hackathon/): What a hackathon is, how to find and join one in India, how to pick a problem, build in 24 to 48 hours, pitch in three minutes and demo without a crash. Written from three first prizes and the judge's table.
- [Smart India Hackathon guide: how SIH works, how to register through your college, choose a problem statement, clear the internal round and present to ministry judges](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/smart-india-hackathon-guide/): What Smart India Hackathon is, how registration works through your institute, how to read and choose a problem statement, what the internal round eliminates most teams on, how to build the prototype and the presentation ministry judges expect, and what happens after. From a builder with three hackathon first prizes and time as a judge.

## Speaking & mentoring

Guest lectures, workshops, tech clubs and mentorship for colleges and communities.

- [How to give a guest lecture in college: preparing a technical talk, handling Q&A, and becoming a speaker colleges invite back](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-give-a-guest-lecture-in-college/): How to get invited to speak at a college, how to prepare a 60- or 90-minute technical session students remember, how to structure slides and demos, how to handle a room that goes quiet or a question you cannot answer, and what turns one talk into repeat invitations. From speaking and mentoring at colleges in Kanpur and running a 500-member developer community.
- [How to improve your public speaking for tech talks: structure, nerves, filler words, and the practice that actually moves the needle](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-improve-public-speaking-for-tech-talks/): Practical public speaking improvement for engineers and students giving technical talks: why content-first practice beats generic public-speaking advice, how to structure a technical talk so a room follows it, handling nerves and filler words, reading a room in real time, and the specific practice routine that improves a talk faster than general public speaking courses.
- [How to invite a guest speaker to your college: the email, the one-pager, fees, logistics and what makes a speaker say yes](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-invite-a-guest-speaker-to-your-college/): A checklist for inviting a guest speaker or guest lecturer to a college event: how to find one, what to put in the first email, whether speakers are paid, what a speaker needs from organisers, how to introduce them, and how to turn one session into a lasting mentor relationship. Written by someone who receives these invitations.
- [How to start a tech community on campus: from five friends to 500 members, the sessions, the structure and the mistakes, from building TechVerse Enclave](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-start-a-tech-community-on-campus/): How to start and grow a student developer community or coding club: the first session, the weekly rhythm that matters more than promotion, roles and leadership handover, getting speakers and sponsors, running hackathons, and what TechVerse Enclave's growth to 500+ members and 200+ mentored students actually looked like.
- [Mentoring students remotely and internationally: what a mentor actually does, how to find one, and how to run a mentorship program across time zones](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/mentoring-students-remotely-and-internationally/): What a good technical mentor does differently from a teacher or a manager, how to find one when your college has no formal program, how to ask well, and how mentoring works once it crosses a time zone: async-first communication, recorded sessions, and running a student mentorship program for a community that spans countries. From mentoring 200-plus students in Kanpur and speaking to international student communities remotely.
- [Personal branding for developers and CS students: building in public, LinkedIn and GitHub that get you hired, and speaking your way into a reputation](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/personal-branding-for-developers/): How a student or early-career engineer builds a reputation that produces internships, clients and speaking invitations: what to post and where, the LinkedIn profile and GitHub that recruiters actually read, writing technical posts without a following, turning projects into talks, and the automation and consistency that make it sustainable. From growing a community to 500+ members and speaking at colleges.

## GenAI careers

Roadmaps, portfolios, interviews and salaries for students and early-career engineers in India.

- [AI final year project ideas for CS, IT, BCA and MCA students: 25 projects that are buildable, demonstrable and get you interviews](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ai-final-year-project-ideas/): Final year project ideas in AI that a student team can actually finish and demo: RAG over college documents, document extraction with validation, face-recognition attendance with a privacy boundary, receipt and prescription readers, a fine-tuned small model, speech-to-text workspaces, and more. For each: what it is, the hard part, the tech, and what makes it stand out. Plus how to pick, how to scope for a semester, what evaluators look for, and how to turn the project into a portfolio piece. From building Annapurna, FaceVision, DocuLens and RAG.NextUpgrad.

## The journey

From a BCA in Kanpur to shipping five production AI apps and leading a 14-member team.

- [Dev.to vs Hashnode vs Medium vs your own blog: where should a developer actually write in 2026?](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/dev-to-vs-hashnode-vs-medium-for-developers/): A practical comparison for developers deciding where to publish technical writing: Dev.to's community and free tier, Hashnode's custom domain and now-paid API, Medium's paywall and algorithm, and a self-hosted blog you fully own. What each costs, who reads each, SEO and discoverability differences, and the two-platform strategy that works for most people: write once, publish to your own site first, syndicate the rest. From publishing across all of them.
- [From a BCA in Kanpur to GenAI engineer: how I got here, what actually mattered, and what I would tell my first-year self](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/from-bca-student-to-genai-engineer/): The honest path from a BCA at VSICS Kanpur to shipping five production AI systems and leading engineering for a 14-member team: the community I built, the hackathons I won and lost, the first clients, the products, and the decisions that compounded. Written for students at colleges nobody has heard of.
- [How to build a developer portfolio website: what to include, what to cut, free hosting, and the three-second test recruiters actually apply](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-a-developer-portfolio-website/): A practical guide to building a personal website as a developer or CS student: the pages it needs, the project write-up format that gets read, what to leave off, free hosting and a custom domain, performance and accessibility basics, and how to keep it updated without it becoming a second job. From building and rebuilding a personal site that anchors a speaking and hiring brand.
- [Turning a student project into a startup: the real signal to look for, what changes, and what most student founders get wrong first](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/turning-a-student-project-into-a-startup/): Most student projects should stay projects. A few have a real signal worth pursuing further: strangers using it without being asked to, a problem that costs someone money or time every week, a founder willing to work on it after the grade or the hackathon prize stops mattering. What actually changes when a project becomes a startup attempt, and the honest test before you commit real time to it.
- [What three hackathon wins and one loss taught me: KrishGyan at IIT Roorkee, BrandHive at CSJMU, Annapurna at MeetKats, and STROT](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-hackathon-wins-and-losses-taught-me/): Four hackathons, told honestly: what we built, why the winners won, why STROT lost, and the specific lessons about scope, users, demos and teams that now shape how I build, mentor and judge. For students who want the version without the highlight reel.

- [Environment variables and config for AI apps: getting API keys right from day one](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/environment-variables-and-config-for-ai-apps/): Hardcoded API keys are the single most common security mistake in student AI projects. A simple config setup that avoids it permanently.
- [Deploying a Python AI app for free: a realistic path from laptop to a working URL](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/deploying-a-python-ai-app-for-free/): You don't need a paid server to put a working AI demo online. A practical path using free tiers, with the trade-offs each one carries.
- [Error handling for flaky LLM APIs: what to do when the provider times out mid-demo](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/error-handling-for-flaky-llm-apis/): LLM provider APIs occasionally time out, rate-limit, or return malformed output. A practical error-handling pattern that keeps your app usable anyway.
- [Caching LLM responses safely: the checklist before you cache anything](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/caching-llm-responses-safely/): Caching cuts cost and latency, but caching the wrong thing serves stale or wrong answers confidently. What's safe to cache and what isn't.
- [Background jobs for slow AI tasks: don't make the user wait on a 30-second request](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/background-jobs-for-slow-ai-tasks/): Some AI tasks — a long document summary, a batch classification — take too long for a synchronous HTTP request. A simple background-job pattern that fixes it.
- [Logging and tracing LLM calls: what a debuggable AI app actually needs](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/logging-and-tracing-llm-calls/): When an AI feature misbehaves in production, print statements won't save you. A practical logging and tracing setup for LLM-backed applications.
- [Rate-limiting your own AI API before your users (or a bug) do it for you](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rate-limiting-an-ai-api-for-students/): One runaway frontend loop can burn a month's API budget in an hour. A simple, practical rate-limiting setup for a student AI project's backend.
- [Deploying a vision model to the edge: quantization and ONNX in practice](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/edge-deployment-for-vision-models-quantized-onnx/): Getting a vision model to run on a phone or low-power device without a cloud round trip: what quantization and ONNX actually buy you, concretely.
- [Five camera-quality problems that quietly break a vision model in production](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/camera-quality-issues-that-break-vision-models/): A model trained on clean, well-lit images meets a real phone camera and fails in ways the demo never showed. What to test for before deployment.
- [From "Living Space Automation" — my first failed project — to five shipped AI apps](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/living-space-automation-to-five-shipped-apps/): Every mentoring session I run starts with the same admission: my first real project failed hard. Here's why that's the part worth telling.
- [Evaluating a vision model beyond accuracy: the metrics that actually predict production behaviour](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/vision-model-evaluation-beyond-accuracy/): A single accuracy number hides which errors a vision model makes and how confidently it makes them. A short list of what to check before shipping.
- [Real-time object detection on a budget GPU: what's actually achievable](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/real-time-object-detection-on-a-budget-gpu/): A realistic frames-per-second budget for object detection on the free or low-cost GPUs students actually have access to, and how to hit it.
- [What I told 100+ first-years at the VSICS Induction](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/vsics-induction-roadmap/): The three-year roadmap I gave incoming engineering students: foundations and AI tools, then hackathons and internships, then placements or a startup.
- [Face-matching thresholds: the trade-off between letting the wrong person in and locking the right one out](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/face-matching-thresholds-false-accept-vs-reject/): Every face-matching system picks a similarity threshold. Set it wrong in either direction and you get a security hole or a support-ticket generator.
- [Building a receipt scanner with a vision LLM: a project walkthrough](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/building-a-receipt-scanner-with-vision-llms/): Extracting merchant, date, line items and total from a photographed receipt using a multimodal model, plus the validation layer that makes it trustworthy.
- [CLIP vs ViT vs a multimodal LLM: picking a vision model without guessing](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/vision-model-choice-clip-vs-vit-vs-multimodal-llm/): Three different families of vision model solve overlapping but distinct problems. A decision guide based on what you're actually trying to build.
- [My journey so far: Dr. Virendra Swarup, IIT Kanpur, IIT Roorkee, CSJMU, and back](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/my-journey-so-far/): A short map of the institutions and teams that shaped the last few years, from a first failed project to co-founding SCULT INDIA.
- [Video frame sampling: you don't need every frame, and processing every frame will bankrupt your project](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/video-frame-sampling-for-vision-models/): Running a vision model on every frame of a video is slow and expensive. A practical sampling strategy that catches what matters without the cost.
- [Handwriting recognition for Indian forms: what makes it harder than printed-text OCR](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/handwriting-recognition-for-indian-forms/): Mixed scripts, inconsistent handwriting and low-quality scans make handwritten form recognition a genuinely different problem from OCR on printed text.
- [Image embeddings for visual search: how 'find similar' actually works](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/image-embeddings-for-visual-search/): The mechanics behind a 'find visually similar items' feature: embedding images into a shared vector space and searching it the same way text RAG does.
- [One base model, five LoRA adapters: serving multiple fine-tuned tasks without five deployments](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/multi-lora-serving-for-multiple-tasks/): Swapping LoRA adapters at request time lets one base model serve several fine-tuned behaviours, instead of hosting a separate full model per task.
- [Fine-tuning checkpoints: what to actually keep, and what to safely delete](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/fine-tuning-checkpoints-what-to-keep/): Saving every epoch's checkpoint fills a disk fast. A practical policy for what to keep, informed by what a loss curve and eval score actually tell you.
- [DPO vs supervised fine-tuning: do student projects need preference tuning at all?](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/dpo-vs-sft-for-student-projects/): Direct Preference Optimization is having a moment. For most student projects, plain supervised fine-tuning on good examples still gets you further, faster.
- [Fine-tuning vs a longer prompt: a real cost comparison](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/fine-tuning-vs-prompting-a-cost-comparison/): A well-engineered prompt with examples can match a fine-tune for far less upfront cost — until volume changes the math. Where the crossover actually sits.
- [Quantizing a fine-tuned model: GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ, and which to pick](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/quantization-after-fine-tuning-gguf-awq-gptq/): A fine-tuned model that doesn't fit your deployment budget needs quantization. The practical differences between the three common formats, in one place.
- [Fine-tuning with 200 examples: what's actually possible](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/fine-tuning-with-limited-labeled-data/): You don't need ten thousand labelled examples to fine-tune usefully. A realistic plan for what 200-2,000 examples can and can't teach a model.
- [Picking a base model to fine-tune in 2026: the checklist I actually use](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/picking-a-base-model-for-fine-tuning-in-2026/): License, size, context length, existing instruction-tuning and community tooling — the factors that matter more than a leaderboard rank when choosing a base model.
- [Fine-tuning for classification vs generation: two different problems wearing the same name](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/fine-tuning-for-classification-vs-generation/): A sentiment classifier and a chatbot both get called 'fine-tuning', but the data format, evaluation and even the model choice differ sharply between them.
- [Catastrophic forgetting: why your fine-tuned model got worse at things you didn't train it on](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/catastrophic-forgetting-in-fine-tuned-models/): A model fine-tuned hard on one narrow task can lose general capability it had before. What causes it and the simplest ways to prevent it in a student project.
- [Synthetic data for fine-tuning: when it works and when it teaches the model your own mistakes](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/synthetic-data-for-fine-tuning-when-it-works/): Generating training examples with a bigger model can fill a data gap fast, or quietly bake in that model's biases and errors. How to tell which you're getting.
- [Self-hosted vs managed vector search: what actually changes at student-project scale](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/self-hosted-vs-managed-vector-search/): pgvector on a free Postgres instance vs a managed vector database — the real trade-offs for a project with under a million vectors, not an enterprise deployment.
- [RAG observability: the five things worth logging (and the ten that aren't)](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rag-observability-what-to-log/): Logging everything drowns the one signal that matters. A short list of what to actually capture from a production retrieval pipeline, and why.
- [The RAG question nobody plans for: 'what if it's just not in the documents?'](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/handling-out-of-scope-questions-in-rag/): A confidence gate catches weak matches, but out-of-scope questions need a different check: does the retrieved context even address the question's topic at all?
- [RAG over a SQL database: why text-to-SQL is a different problem](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rag-with-sql-databases-text-to-sql-patterns/): Vector search doesn't help when the answer is 'run this aggregate query'. A practical pattern for letting an LLM answer questions against a real database safely.
- [Multi-hop questions break single-pass RAG. Here's the pattern that fixes it](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/multi-hop-questions-in-rag-systems/): 'Who won the hackathon the year after X joined?' needs two retrieval steps, not one. A simple decompose-then-retrieve pattern for multi-hop questions.
- [Where a RAG request's latency actually goes (it isn't the LLM call)](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rag-latency-budget-where-time-goes/): Profiling a real RAG endpoint end to end: embedding, vector search, reranking, prompt assembly and generation each take a slice — and the slowest part surprises most people.
- [Teaching AI-powered software development to first-year engineers](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/ai-powered-software-development-session/): Inside the VSICS session where I mapped how AI now touches every stage of the software lifecycle, from requirements to maintenance.
- [Semantic caching for RAG: when it saves money and when it lies to users](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/semantic-cache-for-rag-when-it-helps/): Caching by exact string match misses near-duplicate questions; semantic caching catches them, but a badly-tuned similarity threshold serves stale, wrong answers.
- [RAG for PDFs with tables and images: what breaks and how to fix it](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rag-for-pdfs-with-tables-and-images/): Plain-text chunking destroys tables and ignores images. A practical pipeline for PDFs that actually contain the data your users are asking about.
- [Metadata filtering in RAG: the retrieval fix nobody mentions first](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/metadata-filtering-in-rag-pipelines/): Before you touch embeddings or rerankers, filter by metadata — date, source, document type. It is the cheapest accuracy gain in a retrieval pipeline.
- [I ran the chunk-size experiment so you don't have to: what actually changed](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/rag-chunk-size-experiments-what-actually-works/): Testing 128, 256, 512 and 1024-token chunks on the same retrieval pipeline, with the same eval set, to see which size actually moved recall and answer quality.
- [What a college debate stage taught me about arguing a position I don't hold](https://pranjulrathour.github.io/blog/insight-talk-show-arguing-against-nationalism/): At INSIGHT — The Talk Show, VSICS, I argued against the motion on nationalism and policy. It's a soft-skill exercise every engineer should try.
